title: Researching Investments and Reading the Evidence
intro: Good investment research is mostly about asking the right questions of reliable sources and being honest about what the evidence can and cannot show. This page lists where to find data, gives a process for researching a company or a fund, and explains the statistical traps (backtest overfitting, survivorship bias, data mining) that make so many published strategies fail in practice.

items: Company filings: the SEC's EDGAR database (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K for major events, proxy statements DEF 14A on executive pay and governance, Form 4 for insider trades, 13F for big institutions' holdings). In the UK, Companies House and the RNS news service; in the EU, national regulators and company investor-relations pages.
Earnings calls and presentations: transcripts show what management emphasizes and what analysts worry about.
Fund documents: the prospectus and Key Information Document (fees, strategy, risks), annual reports with full holdings, and the fund's index methodology.
Economic data: FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) for US and many international series; national statistics offices; central bank statements and minutes; the IMF, World Bank, OECD and BIS.
Market data: exchange websites; free sources such as Yahoo Finance and Google Finance (good for prices, less reliable for fundamentals); Morningstar for funds.

Academic data: Kenneth French's data library (factor returns back to 1926), Robert Shiller's online data (S&P 500 prices, dividends, earnings and CAPE since 1871), Aswath Damodaran's datasets (valuations, cost of capital and risk premiums by industry and country), and the Credit Suisse/UBS Global Investment Returns Yearbook (Dimson, Marsh and Staunton) for long-run returns in many countries.

blocks.text: Prefer the original document to someone's summary of it, and the summary of a disinterested party to a sales pitch. Ask of every source: how is it paid, and what would it say if it were wrong?

items: 1. Understand the business. Read the business description and risk factors in the 10-K. What does it sell, to whom, how does it make money, who competes with it?
2. Read ten years of numbers. Revenue growth, margins, ROIC, free cash flow, share count and debt. Look for consistency, and for what changed and why.
3. Judge the moat and the industry. Porter's five forces (rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, supplier power, buyer power) is a useful checklist.
4. Judge management. Track record of capital allocation, how they are paid, insider ownership and trading, candor in letters and calls.
5. Value it several ways (multiples against peers and history, a DCF, a reverse DCF) and write down the assumptions.
6. Write the bear case. What could make this a bad investment? Who is short, and why?
7. Size the position for being wrong, and set a review date.
What exactly does it hold, and what index or process decides that?
Total cost: expense ratio, trading costs (turnover), spread, taxes, any loads or performance fees.

How does its return compare with a cheap index fund of the same style, after costs, over 10+ years? Use a factor regression or at least a style-matched benchmark, not the S&P 500 for a small-cap fund.
How big is it, who runs it, and has the strategy or manager changed?

blocks.text: Fund databases and indexes drop funds and companies that died. Averages of the survivors look better than the full history: studies of mutual funds estimate that survivorship bias inflates average returns by roughly 0.5 to 1.5% a year. The same applies to countries (the US has been the great success story; Russia and China in 1917 and 1949 wiped out investors) and to famous investors (we hear about those who succeeded, not the many who took similar risks and failed).

A backtest applies a rule to historical data to see how it would have done. Try enough rules and some will look brilliant by chance. If you test 20 random strategies, one will on average look 'significant' at the 5% level. Researchers call this data snooping or p-hacking; Bailey and López de Prado's deflated Sharpe ratio (2014) corrects a backtest's Sharpe ratio for the number of strategies tried. Warning signs:

items: Many parameters, or parameters tuned to the exact period tested.
Results that vanish when the start date moves a little or the rule changes slightly.
No allowance for trading costs, taxes, slippage or market impact; trades at prices that weren't available (look-ahead bias: using data that wasn't published yet).
A great Sharpe ratio with no economic story for why the profit exists and why it hasn't been competed away.
No out-of-sample test: the rule should work on data it was not designed on (a later period, other countries, other assets).

blocks.text: Returns are noisy. To tell a manager with a true alpha of 2% a year and 6% tracking error from luck at the usual 95% confidence, you need $t = \alpha\sqrt{T}/\sigma \ge 2$, so $T \ge (2 \times 6/2)^2 = 36$ years. Three- and five-year track records tell you almost nothing about skill. This is also why the persistence of fund performance is so weak.

An anomaly found in one dataset may be a fluke, a risk premium, or a real inefficiency that disappears once known. Hou, Xue and Zhang (2020) tried to replicate 452 published anomalies and found most failed once tiny stocks were handled properly. Prefer findings that hold across many countries and decades, have a plausible risk or behavioral explanation, and survive after publication.

Economists' and strategists' market forecasts have poor records: year-ahead S&P 500 targets are clustered near 'up about 8%' and routinely miss by more than the forecast itself. Philip Tetlock's work on expert political judgment and 'superforecasters' found that pundits who were confident and famous did worse than modest, probability-minded forecasters who updated often. Treat long-run capital market assumptions (expected returns from valuations and yields) as useful ranges for planning, and short-run predictions as entertainment.

blocks.title: Is it skill?
blocks.text: A fund beat its benchmark by 3% a year for 5 years with a tracking error of 8%. What is the t-statistic? Is this convincing evidence of skill?
solution: $IR = 3/8 = 0.375$; $t = 0.375 \times \sqrt{5} \approx 0.84$. Far below 2: a record like this would arise by luck alone quite often. It is not convincing.

blocks.title: Many trials
blocks.text: A researcher tests 100 trading rules on the same data, none of which really works, at a 5% significance level. How many would you expect to look 'significant'? What could the researcher do?
solution: About 5. Corrections: require a stricter threshold (Bonferroni: 0.05/100 = 0.0005, or a t-statistic above about 3.5), report how many rules were tried, and test the winners on data held out from the start.
